Draft the Objective section from the following consultation dialogue:

[doctor]: Good morning, John. How are you feeling today?[patient]: Not too well, doctor. I've been having severe chest pain for the past 5 days.[doctor]: I'm sorry to hear that. Can you describe the chest pain for me?[patient]: It's constant and gets worse when I take deep breaths or cough.[doctor]: I see. You mentioned it's affecting your sleep and daily activities, correct?[patient]: Yes, it really has. I can barely sleep at night because of the pain.[doctor]: Any other symptoms you've noticed?[patient]: I've also had shortness of breath, a dry cough, and a fever.[doctor]: Hmm, fever too. How high has the fever been?[patient]: It's been pretty high. I haven't measured it every time, but it's definitely there.[doctor]: Alright, let's go through some more questions. Have you noticed any weight loss recently?[patient]: No, no weight loss.[doctor]: Any palpitations or dizziness?[patient]: No, none of that.[doctor]: How about nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain?[patient]: No, nothing like that.[doctor]: Any joint pain or swelling?[patient]: No, my joints are fine.[doctor]: Any headaches, dizziness, or neurological issues?[patient]: No, none at all.[doctor]: Okay, let's check your vital signs. Your blood pressure is 128 over 76 mmHg, heart rate is 92 bpm, respiratory rate is 20 breaths per minute, and your temperature is 101.2°F. Your oxygen saturation is 95% on room air.[patient]: Alright.[doctor]: I'm going to do a physical examination now. Let me start by listening to your lungs. Take a deep breath in and out for me.[patient]: (Breathing deeply)[doctor]: I hear diminished breath sounds and a pleural friction rub over your left lower lung fields. No wheezing or crackles, though.[patient]: Is that bad?[doctor]: It indicates some inflammation in the lining of the lungs, which could be pleurisy. Let me check your heart sounds now. (Listening) Your heart sounds are normal, no murmurs or rubs. I'll check your abdomen next. It's soft and non-tender, no signs of any issues there. And your extremities show no edema or cyanosis.[patient]: Okay.[doctor]: I want to get a chest X-ray and some blood tests, including a CBC and CRP, to confirm the diagnosis and check for any infection or inflammation.[patient]: Alright.[doctor]: In the meantime, I'm going to prescribe you some medications. I'll give you ibuprofen 600 mg, which you should take three times a day for 7 days to help with the pain and inflammation.[patient]: Okay, I can do that.[doctor]: If the tests suggest an infection, I'll also prescribe amoxicillin 500 mg, to be taken three times a day for 7 days.[patient]: Got it.[doctor]: We'll schedule a follow-up appointment in 1 week to see how you're doing and adjust the treatment if needed.[patient]: Alright, sounds good.[doctor]: If your symptoms persist or worsen, I'll refer you to a pulmonologist for further evaluation and management.[patient]: I hope it doesn't come to that.[doctor]: Let's hope not. But it's good to have a plan in place. Do you have any questions for me?[patient]: No, I think you've covered everything.[doctor]: Great. Make sure to rest, stay hydrated, and take your medications as prescribed. If your symptoms worsen or new symptoms develop, come back to the clinic immediately.[patient]: Will do, doctor. Thank you.[doctor]: You're welcome, John. Take care and get well soon.[patient]: Thanks, doctor. I'll try my best.

**Vital Signs:**- BP: 128/76 mmHg- HR: 92 bpm- RR: 20 breaths per minute- Temp: 101.2°F (38.4°C)- SpO2: 95% on room air**Physical Examination:**- **General:** Alert, cooperative, appears distressed due to pain.- **Respiratory:** Diminished breath sounds and pleural friction rub noted over the left lower lung fields. No wheezing or crackles.- **Cardiovascular:** Heart sounds normal, no murmurs or rubs.- **Abdomen:** Soft, non-tender, no hepatosplenomegaly.- **Extremities:** No edema, no cyanosis.

[doctor]: Hi Mr. Doe, how are you today?[patient]: Hello, doctor. I'm doing alright. Thanks for seeing me.[doctor]: Of course. I see you're here for right shoulder pain. Can you tell me more about what's been going on?[patient]: Yeah, I've had pretty bad pain in my right shoulder for about four weeks now. It's really messing with my daily stuff.[doctor]: I'm sorry to hear that. How would you describe the pain? Is it constant or does it come and go?[patient]: It's constant. Makes it tough to move my shoulder and do things like gardening, dressing, and cooking.[doctor]: I understand. Have you noticed any other symptoms associated with the shoulder pain?[patient]: Yeah, I've got some muscle loss and sometimes my fingers tingle.[doctor]: Muscle atrophy and tingling, got it. How about your sleep? Has the pain affected your sleep in any way?[patient]: Yep, it has. I'm only getting about 5 to 6 hours of sleep a night because of it.[doctor]: That sounds very challenging. Have you tried any treatments or medications for the pain?[patient]: Just some over-the-counter pain meds, but they haven't really helped.[doctor]: Okay. Let's review a few things. Do you have any other systemic symptoms like fever, weight loss, or night sweats?[patient]: No, none of those.[doctor]: Thank you for clarifying. Let's move on to your review of systems. For musculoskeletal, you've mentioned decreased range of motion, muscle atrophy, and shoulder pain. For neurological, you've mentioned occasional tingling in the fingers. Any other symptoms you'd like to mention?[patient]: No, I think that's everything.[doctor]: Great, let's move on to your vital signs. Your blood pressure today is 130/80 mmHg, heart rate is 72 bpm, respiratory rate is 18 bpm, temperature is 98.6°F, and your oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. [patient]: Okay.[doctor]: Let's proceed with a physical examination. I'll be calling out my findings as we go along. First, on inspection, I notice noticeable muscle atrophy in the right shoulder with mild swelling. Does that sound right?[patient]: Yes, that's correct.[doctor]: When I palpate the shoulder, there's significant tenderness over the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. How does that feel?[patient]: It hurts quite a bit when you press there.[doctor]: I understand. In terms of range of motion, you have severely limited movement, particularly in shoulder abduction and external rotation. Is that what you've been experiencing?[patient]: Yes, it's very hard to move my shoulder in those directions.[doctor]: There's also marked weakness in shoulder flexion and external rotation. Now, I'm going to perform some special tests. The Drop Arm Test, Hawkins-Kennedy Test, and Scapular Winging are all positive. [patient]: What does that mean?[doctor]: These tests suggest that you may have a rotator cuff tear or rupture. We need further imaging to confirm this. [patient]: I see.[doctor]: We'll be conducting a CBC and metabolic panel to check for any underlying conditions, and we're also awaiting the results of an X-ray of your right shoulder.[patient]: Okay.[doctor]: Based on your symptoms and the physical exam findings, our primary diagnosis is an unspecified rotator cuff tear or rupture of the right shoulder.[patient]: That sounds serious.[doctor]: It can be, but we're going to work on a treatment plan for you. For medications, I'll be prescribing Methocarbamol 750 mg, oral, three times daily for muscle spasms. You should continue with your albuterol and fluticasone inhalers for your COPD management.[patient]: Got it.[doctor]: We'll need a follow-up in 4 weeks to review your blood work and X-ray results. Depending on those results, we might need to consider potential surgical intervention.[patient]: Alright.[doctor]: I'm also referring you to an orthopedic surgeon, Dr. Alan Brown, for a surgical evaluation pending your next visit.[patient]: Okay, thank you.[doctor]: If your symptoms persist or worsen, we'll order an MRI of your right shoulder to get a more detailed view.[patient]: Understood.[doctor]: In the meantime, engage in gentle shoulder exercises as tolerated and avoid lifting heavy objects. Additionally, consider making dietary changes to include more fresh produce to improve your overall health.[patient]: I'll do that.[doctor]: Do you have any questions for me?[patient]: No, I think you've covered everything.[doctor]: Alright, Mr. Doe. Remember to contact the clinic if your symptoms worsen or if you develop any new symptoms. We'll see you in 4 weeks for a follow-up.[patient]: Thank you, doctor.[doctor]: You're welcome. Take care, Mr. Doe.

**Vital Signs:**- Blood Pressure: 130/80 mmHg- Heart Rate: 72 bpm- Respiratory Rate: 18 bpm- Temperature: 98.6°F- Oxygen Saturation: 95% on room air**Physical Examination:**- Inspection: Noticeable muscle atrophy in the right shoulder with mild swelling.- Palpation: Significant tenderness over the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles.- Range of Motion: Severely limited, particularly in shoulder abduction and external rotation.- Strength Testing: Marked weakness in shoulder flexion and external rotation.- Special Tests: Positive Drop Arm Test, Hawkins-Kennedy Test, and Scapular Winging.**Pending Investigations:**- X-ray of the right shoulder: Awaiting results.

[patient] Okay, that sounds good.[doctor] In terms of medication, we'll continue you on Methotrexate 20 mg orally once weekly for maintenance therapy and Folic Acid 1 mg daily to reduce side effects from Methotrexate.[patient] Got it.[doctor] It's really important that you adhere to your medication schedule and keep up with your follow-up appointments. We may need to adjust your medication.[patient] Okay, I understand.[doctor] Great. Thank you for coming in today. Keep up the good work with your physiotherapy and take care of yourself. We’ll see you in a month.[patient] Thanks, Doctor. See you next time.[doctor] Take care.
